nameStory: Eastern Tree-mallow gets its name from its tall, tree-like stature compared to its low-growing mallow cousins - it can tower up to 6 feet tall! The 'Eastern' part refers to its native range in eastern Europe and southwestern Asia, though it occasionally appears as a garden escape in New England.
description: Eastern Tree-mallow is a tall, upright flowering plant that can reach an impressive 6 feet in height. It's covered in soft, grayish hairs that give the whole plant a downy, silvery appearance. Throughout summer, it produces lovely pink flowers that are much larger than most other mallows, each bloom stretching 1-2 inches across with five delicate petals.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large pink flowers, 1-2 inches across, with five silky petals that feel papery to the touch. The flowers have a prominent central column of fused stamens typical of the mallow family.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palmate leaves (shaped like an open hand) with 3-5 rounded lobes, up to 3.5 inches long and wide. They feel distinctly soft and fuzzy due to dense grayish hairs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright, growing up to 6 feet high with multiple stems. The entire plant has a silvery-green appearance from the downy hairs covering stems and leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, flat seed cases arranged in a circle (called a schizocarp) that split into wedge-shaped segments when ripe, typical of the mallow family.

habitat: Eastern Tree-mallow is extremely rare in New England, typically found as an occasional garden escape near cultivated areas. When it does appear, it prefers sunny, well-drained soils in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, or the edges of gardens.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with characteristic fuzzy, grayish-green leaves. Young plants form basal rosettes before sending up tall flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with showy pink flowers appearing continuously. The soft, downy leaves are at their most distinctive during active growing season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, followed by the development of round, segmented seed cases. Leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level as a herbaceous perennial, leaving no above-ground traces for identification.

funFact: With only one recorded observation in all of New England, spotting an Eastern Tree-mallow here would be like finding botanical gold - you'd likely be looking at a garden escapee that's incredibly rare in our region!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Common Mallow or Musk Mallow, but Eastern Tree-mallow towers over these relatives at up to 6 feet tall versus their typical 1-3 feet. Remember: if it's a giant among mallows with silvery-fuzzy leaves, you might have found our rare Eastern Tree-mallow.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly classified in the genus Lavatera, so you might find it listed in older field guides as Lavatera thuringiaca. Botanists moved it to the Malva genus based on genetic studies, but the name change is relatively recent.
compareHints: Eastern Tree-mallow stands out from other mallows in New England primarily by its exceptional height - it can reach 6 feet compared to the 1-3 feet typical of Musk Mallow or Common Mallow. Its flowers are also notably larger at 1-2 inches across, and the entire plant has a distinctive silvery appearance from dense grayish hairs that's much more pronounced than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mallows, musk mallow stands out with its deeply-cut, narrow leaf segments - quite different from the broad, rounded leaves of common mallow or the small, kidney-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.
Unlike its cousin musk mallow which grows upright with deeply divided leaves, dwarf mallow stays low and sprawling with round, shallowly-lobed leaves.

Among its mallow relatives, greater musk-mallow stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - they're cut almost to the midrib unlike the merely lobed leaves of common mallow or the heart-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.
Common mallow stands out from other New England mallows by being the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most intensely colored flowers.
Unlike the perennial musk mallow with its deeply divided leaves and smaller flowers, Royal Mallow is an annual with simpler heart-shaped leaves and much larger blooms.
Among New England's mallows, cheeseweed mallow is distinguished by having the smallest flowers and the smoothest seed pods.
